title: The role of the international FinTech market in shaping investment support for global food security
summary: The article aims to substantiate the role of the international FinTech market in shaping investment provision for global food security and to identify the channels through which digital financial technologies can transform access to capital in the agri-food sector. The research uses systems analysis, scientific generalization, comparison, classification, structural and logical analysis, and conceptual modeling. The study establishes that digital payment systems, digital lending, peer-to-peer financing, crowdfunding, digital investment platforms, InsurTech, artificial intelligence, big data, distributed ledger technologies, and RegTech can expand financial inclusion, diversify sources of investment capital, reduce selected transaction costs and information asymmetry, improve risk assessment and insurance, and facilitate cross-border financial flows. It is demonstrated that the impact of FinTech on global food security is predominantly indirect and is realized through an investment channel: the development of the international FinTech market creates new financing opportunities; these opportunities are transformed into investments in agricultural production, processing, storage, logistics, digitalization, climate adaptation and risk management; such investments enhance the productivity and resilience of agri-food systems and contribute to the physical and economic accessibility and stability of food supply. The scientific novelty lies in the substantiation of an integrated mechanism “FinTech – investment – agri-food system – food security”, which combines financial accessibility, capital mobilization, productive investment and the resulting parameters of food-system resilience within a single causal framework. The practical significance of the findings lies in their potential use by public authorities, financial institutions, international organizations, investors, and agri-food enterprises when designing investment instruments and programs to improve access to finance and strengthen food-system resilience. Particular attention is paid to the constraints of digital inequality, cybersecurity risks, regulatory fragmentation, and differences in institutional capacity. Further research should quantitatively assess the relationship between FinTech development, international investment flows, and food-security indicators, and test the proposed mechanism across countries with different levels of digital and financial development. title: A Data-Driven Framework for Measuring CSR Effectiveness and Advancing Sustainable Business Processes
summary: The increasing focus on sustainability has heightened recognition of the importance of data-driven approaches to accurately assess and enhance the effectiveness of “Corporate Social Responsibility” (CSR). The research examines the application of data-centric technology to assess the efficacy of CSR. This research reviewed the current literature on the concepts of “Artificial Intelligence” (AI), “Machine Learning” (ML), “Business Intelligence” (BI), “Business Process Management” (BPM), advanced analytics and the incorporation of ESG into organizations to understand how a data-driven approach can enhance CSR evaluation and the sustainability of organizations. According to the literature examined, AI decision models can be used to prioritize CSR programs, while advanced analytics and BI tools can support the evaluation and reporting of ESG performance. Data-driven BPM and Industry 4.0 technologies aid in process optimization and sustainability. Nevertheless, numerous obstacles have been recognized in the literature, including a lack of standardized CSR metrics, poor data quality and availability, fragmented data, inconsistent disclosure practices, governance limitations, regulatory issues, and greenwashing. The critique highlights the importance of addressing the gap in combining the elements of CSR evaluation, data analytics, transparency, stakeholders, and sustainable business operations. Thus, the proposed conceptual framework seeks to integrate reliable CSR information, metrics, analytics, disclosure practices, and stakeholders' concerns to enhance productivity and organizational effectiveness. This document establishes a basis for entities aiming to adopt more transparent, quantifiable, and data-driven CSR initiatives

title: FinTech Mergers and Acquisitions in India: Rethinking Competition and Regulatory Oversight in the Age of AI
summary: This paper explores the need for a contestation and regulation framework in India to meet the pace of mergers and acquisitions (M&A) in the FinTech sector in view of the growth of financial innovation powered by AI. The question we raise: How can Indian competition law and financial regulation evolve to make digital finance competitive and accountable? To tackle this, we have conducted doctrinal and comparative analysis of contemporary law, and recent reform and case studies. The point is identified as a key gap: traditional thresholds for mergers are not always sufficient to encompass "killer acquisitions" of young, promising FinTech companies by established incumbents, particularly with respect to AI and "data" technologies. This is a significant move to bridge this gap with the new "deal value threshold" (DVT) framework for global acquisitions more than ₹2,000 crore, subject to the approval of the CCI, which mandates approval of the acquisition, when the target has significant operations in India. However, there are some questions that need to be addressed: What constitutes "substantial operations?" and, of course, AI and data analytics issues await further clarity. Our literature review and legal analysis include legal and policy provisions of the Competition Act 2002/2023; the Competition Commission of India (CCI) Reports and Regulations; SEBI and RBI reports and policy papers on FinTech/AI; and important developments from international regulatory bodies. We provide an analysis of Indian and EU/US legal frameworks and examine transaction value tests used in Germany and HSR filing thresholds, as well as new antitrust principles on anticompetitive acquisitions in the US. title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED ENTERPRISES (SMES): AN INTEGRATIVE SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
summary: With the adoption of digital transformation in SMEs, it was possible to identify several contributions of digital business strategies, which are proving increasingly necessary in a constantly evolving corporate environment. This research aims to identify, through the studies, the main contributions of digital transformations in small and medium-sized enterprises over the last 10 years. The methodology used was an integrative systematic literature review, conducted through the multidisciplinary Web of Science database. To analyze the 33 articles, the synthesis matrix developed by Botelho, Cunha and Macedo (2011) was used. The results made it possible to identify some points relevant to the topic, such as the term Digitalization, used to refer to Digital Transformation. Regarding the challenges and opportunities faced by SMEs, a common point is the resistance many of them show to adopting new contemporary updates.

title: Digital Transformation of Retail and Distribution Channels in Advanced Manufacturing: An Evidence-Calibrated Framework Applied to Pak Elektron Limited
summary: Public descriptions of digital transformation often reveal customer interfaces more readily than the systems connecting them to production and distribution. This paper develops the Digital Manufacturing-to-Market Ecosystem (DM2ME), a six-domain architecture for examining those connections while recording capability maturity separately from the evidence supporting it. A bounded documentary application to Pak Elektron Limited distinguishes corporate infrastructure from its Appliances and Power businesses. The 2025 annual report describes current enterprise resource planning (ERP) integration, manufacturing information systems, reporting tools and technology governance; these disclosures support corporate-level classifications that cannot be inferred from customer-facing websites alone. Appliances provides observable retail and service interfaces, while Power has a reported digital transformer lifecycle initiative. Dealer integration, division-specific system coverage, predictive-model use and adaptive feedback remain only partly observable. Classifications represent the highest level supported by the available documents, rather than estimates of the firm's actual capability ceiling. The contribution is a transparent procedure for stating what an external assessment can establish, how business-unit scope affects inference, and which evidence would justify a stronger claim. The application illustrates the procedure but does not validate a measurement scale or identify causal performance effects. Independent coding, internal process evidence and comparative fieldwork are required before DM2ME can support maturity benchmarking.

title: Legal Protection of Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT) In Indonesia: An Analysis of the Regulatory Framework and Legal Issues in Electronic Transactions
summary: The rapid development of information and communication technology has transformed financial transaction systems through the implementation of Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT). This system enables fund transfers to be conducted quickly, efficiently, and in real time without direct physical interaction. As an essential component of the digital economy, EFT supports digital banking, fintech services, and e-commerce transactions. However, its implementation also creates various legal challenges, including issues related to data security, system reliability, legal liability, and consumer protection. Risks may arise from technical failures as well as cybercrimes such as fraud, unauthorized access, and misuse of personal data. This study aims to analyze the concept and legal framework of EFT in Indonesia and identify legal issues arising from its implementation. Using a normative juridical method with statutory and conceptual approaches, the study finds that existing regulations remain fragmented and insufficiently integrated. Therefore, regulatory harmonization and stronger legal protection are needed to ensure legal certainty and public trust in digital financial transactions.

title: Precarity, Labor Governance, and Career Adaptability in Decent Work Studies
summary: This systematic mapping review examines how Decent Work (DW) has been studied through three complementary lenses: Precarity/Uncertainty, Labor Governance, and Career Adaptability. A search covering 2017–2023 across SAGE Journals, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, and ScienceDirect produced a final corpus of thirty-two peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2023. Eligible studies used DW as a substantive construct, framework, outcome, or analytical lens; each study was assigned to one primary thematic domain for descriptive counting. The largest cluster concerned Precarity/Uncertainty (fifteen studies; 46.9%), followed by Career Adaptability (eleven studies; 34.4%) and Labor Governance (six studies; 18.8%). Precarity research foregrounded the structural production and lived experience of insecurity. Labor Governance research examined institutional rules, supply-chain power, worker participation, corporate governance, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) assessment. Career Adaptability research concentrated on individual resources and outcomes within unequal opportunity structures. The journal distribution suggests partial clustering across publication communities, although the review did not conduct formal discipline-level coding. The review proposes a non-causal macro–meso–micro analytical framework and an illustrative measurement schema linking objective employment conditions, perceived DW, governance mechanisms, and worker resources and outcomes. The findings support cross-level research designs while underscoring that adaptive resources cannot substitute for rights, social protection, worker voice, or enforcement.

title: Building competitive advantage through digital transformation: How market turbulence shapes performance outcomes in Indonesian SMEs
summary: This study examines competitive advantage's mediating role in digital transformation-firm performance relationships while investigating market turbulence's moderating effect, addressing gaps in understanding environmental volatility's influence on transformation effectiveness in emerging markets. Survey data from 350 Indonesian SMEs were analyzed using PLS-SEM and Necessary Condition Analysis. Results reveal competitive advantage partially mediates digital transformation-performance relationships, transmitting 30% of total effects through indirect pathways. Market turbulence significantly moderates transformation processes with progressive effect intensification across turbulence levels. NCA demonstrates that competitive advantage, digital transformation, and market turbulence constitute necessary conditions creating performance ceilings rather than merely additive contributors. Organizations must simultaneously develop competitive positioning, transformation capabilities, and appropriate environmental contexts, as deficiency in any factor generates insurmountable performance ceilings. This research reconciles contradictory literature by demonstrating digital transformation operates through dual pathways with contingent effectiveness, providing empirically validated framework explaining when and how digital transformation creates value through moderated mediation and necessary condition logic.

title: Betting on Homes
summary: In this paper, we analyze the differences in annualized capital gains across heterogeneous investor groups in the US housing market, namely owner-occupiers, private investors, as well as short- and long-term institutional investors. Our empirical results link the performance differences to heterogeneity in risk-taking. In particular, investor-specific exposure to lagged local return dispersion explains persistent performance differences of investors within a given market. Short-term institutional investors outperform others by exploiting the upside potential of local return dispersion. By contrast, neither macroeconomic fundamentals nor local factors, such as momentum and downside risk, can explain the observed performance disparities.

title: Environmental Disclosure Research Revisited: A Bibliometric–TCCM Synthesis of Theoretical Integration and Methodological Diversification
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the evolution and determinants of corporate environmental disclosure research through a systematic review of 117 peer‐reviewed articles published from 2016 to 2026 in Scopus. Using the PRISMA 2020 protocol and the SPAR‐4‐SLR framework, a bibliometric analysis was conducted with Bibliometrix and VOSviewer, complemented by the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Method (TCCM) approach to map the intellectual structure, thematic development and research gaps. The findings indicate growing research output, rising markedly after 2023, with China leading in publication output and the United Kingdom attracting the greatest citation impact. Legitimacy, stakeholder and institutional theories dominate the field but are often used in parallel rather than integrated, while governance mechanisms and firm‐level characteristics show inconsistent associations across contexts. Thematic analysis identifies environmental reporting as the core theme, whereas disclosure quality, green innovation and performance outcomes remain underexplored. Future research should prioritise theoretical integration, disclosure quality measurement and methodologically diverse designs.

title: Sustainable Value Creation and Board Gender Diversity in Multinational Enterprises: The Moderating Role of Degree of Internationalisation
summary: ABSTRACT This study explores the empirical relationship between sustainable value creation (SVC), board gender diversity (BGD) and the degree of internationalisation (DOI) in multinational enterprises (MNEs). Using an unbalanced panel of 285 MNEs across 22 countries over the period 2016–2025 and employing high‐dimensional fixed effects (FE), system GMM and entropy balancing techniques, we find that the individual effects of BGD and DOI on SVC are negative and insignificant, respectively. However, the interaction term (BGD × DOI) has a positive and significant effect on SVC. Theoretically, our findings suggest that the rigorous monitoring associated with gender‐diverse boards shifts from being a coordination cost to a value‐enhancing asset as MNEs face the heightened complexity and information asymmetry of global operations. This study contributes to Sustainability, Corporate Governance and International Business literature by synthesising stakeholder and legitimacy perspectives to explain the contingent role of corporate governance in MNE sustainable value creation.

title: Strengthening the Quality Education Strategy (SDG 4) through a Digital Transformation Strategy in Selected Iraqi Universities
summary: Purpose: This study examines the role of digital transformation strategy in strengthening quality education outcomes aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) in selected Iraqi public universities. Design/Methodology/Approach: A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed. Data were collected from 237 academic leaders across three Iraqi universities using a structured questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and linear regression analysis were conducted to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings: The results reveal a significant positive relationship between the availability of digital transformation requirements and quality education indicators (β=0.744; R²=0.617; p < 0.05). While digital infrastructure readiness was high, organisational and training-related barriers remain substantial. Original/Value of the Paper: The originality of this study stems from filling a research gap concerning the role of digital transformation in enhancing the quality of education and achieving SDG 4 in Iraqi higher education. It also provides empirical evidence that contributes to enriching the scientific literature and offers practical guidance for universities and policymakers. title: AUDITING FINANCIAL STATEMENTS AND IDENTIFYING FRAUD RISKS IN ENTERPRISES
summary: In the modern business environment, the reliability and transparency of financial statements are essential for maintaining stakeholder confidence, ensuring effective corporate governance, and supporting sustainable economic development. However, enterprises may face various financial reporting risks, including intentional misstatements, asset misappropriation, manipulation of accounting records, and fraudulent financial transactions. This article examines the importance of financial statement auditing in identifying and preventing fraud risks within enterprises. It explores the main types of financial fraud, the role of internal control systems, and the application of analytical procedures and risk-based auditing methods. Particular attention is given to the responsibilities of external and internal auditors, the use of digital technologies in fraud detection, and the importance of professional skepticism. The study concludes that an effective audit process, supported by transparent accounting practices and strong internal controls, can significantly reduce the likelihood of financial fraud and improve the quality of corporate financial reporting.

title: Beyond the basics: how digital transformation, orientation and competence fuel SME performance through resilience in the manufacturing sector
summary: Purpose In emerging economies such as Pakistan, SMEs have a high failure rate, underscoring the need to understand what drives SME performance. This paper fills a knowledge gap by considering the impact of digital transformation, entrepreneurial orientation, entrepreneurial competencies and entrepreneurial resilience on SMEs' performance. Entrepreneurial resilience serves as a mediator between digital transformation, entrepreneurial orientation, entrepreneurial competencies and SME performance. Finally, environmental dynamism (ED) is used as a moderator between entrepreneurial resilience and SMEs' performance. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 453 managers of manufacturing SMEs in Punjab, Pakistan. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling is used for hypothesis testing. Findings Digital transformation, entrepreneurial orientation and entrepreneurial competencies have a significant and positive influence on entrepreneurial resilience and SME performance. Entrepreneurial resilience significantly enhances SMEs' performance. Additionally, entrepreneurial resilience significantly mediates the relationships among digital transformation, entrepreneurial orientation, entrepreneurial competencies and SME performance. Finally, ED significantly moderates the relationship between entrepreneurial resilience and SMEs' performance. Practical implications SME managers should prioritize digital transformation, entrepreneurial orientation, competence, resilience and ED to measure SMEs' performance. Policymakers can support these efforts by developing adaptive frameworks that enable SMEs to remain competitive in dynamic environments. Originality/value This is initial research that integrates digital transformation, entrepreneurial orientation, entrepreneurial competence, entrepreneurial resilience and ED to examine SME performance within the resource orchestration theory (ROT).

title: Bridging micro-actions and macro-transitions: Diagnosing socio-technical change from a quarter-century of significant corporate developments in FinTech
summary: This study introduces a framework that uses news-based organizational events as signals to diagnose socio-technical transitions. I examine a unique longitudinal dataset of daily corporate developments in the global FinTech industry from 1999 to 2025. The findings show that patterns in strategic actions map to four distinct transition phases: emergence , acceleration , industrialization , and stabilization . Each phase exhibits a distinct financial signature. The acceleration phase is particularly notable for combining the highest returns with the highest systematic risk, consistent with a high-risk, high-return profile. The analysis also reveals non-linear phase effects with optimal concentration ranges. For returns, the relationship with phase concentration is inverted U-shaped, peaking at 23.94% for emergence. For geographic diversification, the pattern is U-shaped, indicating that deeper transition engagement ultimately accelerates global expansion. Exogenous crises are associated with accelerated transition dynamics: showing increased emergence and industrialization while acceleration declines. By linking firm-level actions to system-level financial outcomes, the framework bridges the micro-macro divide in transition theory. It offers managers and policymakers a real-time diagnostic lens for navigating technological change. The analysis establishes a strong empirical foundation for future predictive models, though the current results identify only contemporaneous associations, not predictive causality.

title: Dynamic Capabilities, Organizational Resilience, Digital Transformation and Organizational Performance of Deposit-Taking Saccos in Nairobi County, Kenya
summary: This study examined the influence of dynamic capabilities on the organizational performance of deposit-taking SACCOs in Nairobi County, Kenya, and tested the mediating role of organizational resilience and the moderating role of digital transformation. Given the importance of SACCOs and the various challenges they face from digital disruption and regulation, this study aims to investigate the impact of dynamic capabilities on the performance of SACCOs in Kenya’s Nairobi County. The survey design was used to collect data directly from the SACCO managers in the study areas. Out of the 240 questionnaires distributed, 210 yielded usable responses for the study, giving the study an 87.50% response rate. The data were collected using five-point Likert scales and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, hierarchical regression, Hayes PROCESS Models 4 (mediation), 1 (moderation), 14 (moderated mediation), and 59 (second-stage moderated mediation). The findings of the study revealed that dynamic capabilities had a positive and significant effect on organizational performance. Furthermore, dynamic capabilities significantly enhanced the organizational resilience of these SACCOs, and the organizational resilience significantly improved their organizational performance. Additionally, digital transformation significantly predicted their organizational performance. The study also established that organizational resilience partially mediated the relationship between dynamic capabilities and the performance of these SACCOs. The index for moderated mediation was significant, as digital transformation significantly moderated the relationship between dynamic capabilities and the organizational performance of these SACCOs. The findings of this study showed that deposit-taking SACCOs in Nairobi County perform better if they have dynamic capabilities that translate to organizational resilience that is further enhanced through digital transformation. For better organizational performance by SACCO managers, there is the need to strengthen their dynamic capabilities and institute systems that improve their organizational resilience and align their digital systems with their organizational objectives.

title: Social Disintegration of Society: Purposelessness, the Crisis of Social Trust, and the Fate of Human Values under Conditions of Digital Transformation
summary: This theoretical-conceptual article examines the phenomenon of social disintegration in contemporary society through the lenses of purposelessness, the weakening of social trust, economic transformation, digital information environments, and intergenerational historical memory. Integrating sociological and philosophical frameworks from Émile Durkheim, Leo Tolstoy, George Orwell, and Chingiz Aitmatov, the study explores the evolving dynamics of social trust, moral responsibility, and institutional justice. Furthermore, it introduces a working concept of "Intellectual Stability"—defined as an individual's interconnected capacity for critical thinking, epistemic humility, independent judgment, and moral responsibility amidst digital information flows—and puts forward five testable hypotheses regarding social trust, economic interests, and historical memory for future empirical investigation. title: Recent Developments in the Regulation of Corporate Ethics in India
summary: Corporate ethics play a critical role in maintaining transparency, accountability, and sustainability in businesses. In India, corporate governance has evolved significantly in response to high-profile scandals and the growing need for ethical conduct in the corporate sector. This article examines the recent regulatory changes aimed at strengthening corporate ethics, including amendments to the Companies Act, SEBI regulations on disclosures, the prohibition of insider trading, and the strengthening of independent directors' roles. The introduction of National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC) and enhanced whistleblower protections also emphasize the promotion of ethical practices. Furthermore, ESG reporting mandates and the impact of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) highlight India's focus on responsible corporate behavior. While challenges in enforcement persist, these developments mark a decisive step towards building an ethical and transparent corporate ecosystem in India.

title: Do financial technologies contribute to improving universal health coverage? A spatial analysis of WAEMU countries
summary: Abstract Context In developing countries, digital financial services are emerging as essential levers for addressing low health coverage and regional disparities. This study analyzes the contribution of the adoption of financial technologies (Fintech) to universal health coverage (UHC) in the WAEMU zone. Methods The study uses spatial econometrics and examines data from 2011 to 2021 from the World Bank, the BCEAO, and the WHO. A spatial Durbin model (SDM) was used to capture direct and indirect spatial spillover effects between member countries after detecting spatial autocorrelation. Results The results show that Financial Technology (Fintech) has significant spatial effects, strengthening universal health coverage through technology diffusion and reduced transaction costs. The estimated direct, indirect and total effects of Fintech are respectively 0.022, 0.011 and 0.033, suggesting that Fintech adoption is associated with both within-country and cross-border spatial effects. Conclusions To leverage digital services for healthcare development, WAEMU authorities must prioritize digital infrastructure and strengthen the quality of institutions through robust regulatory frameworks. This regional integration of financial technologies represents a model for improving healthcare in emerging markets, driven by globalization.

title: Dynamics and Fragilities of the Moroccan Entrepreneurial Ecosystem: From Seeding to Sustainable Growth
summary: The Moroccan entrepreneurial ecosystem has experienced significant growth over the last decade through the expansion of public policies, startup support structures, incubators, accelerators, and investment initiatives aimed at stimulating innovation and economic diversification. Entrepreneurship is increasingly considered a strategic lever for job creation, technological modernization, and social inclusion. However, despite the multiplication of programs encouraging business creation, the sustainability of startups and their transition from early-stage development to long-term growth remain major challenges. This article analyzes the dynamics and structural fragilities of the Moroccan entrepreneurial ecosystem by examining its institutional foundations, performance indicators, and systemic barriers. The study highlights the paradox between strong support for startup creation and the limited mechanisms ensuring post-creation sustainability. Using insights from international rankings and reports such as the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) and StartupBlink, the article evaluates Morocco’s global entrepreneurial positioning and identifies both strengths and weaknesses within the ecosystem. Particular attention is devoted to issues related to bureaucracy, access to finance, entrepreneurial education, research and development transfer, and regional disparities. The paper also explores emerging signals of ecosystem maturity through successful Moroccan startups operating in sectors such as digital health, fintech, trade technology, and sustainable innovation. Finally, the article proposes strategic recommendations focused on educational reform, long-term entrepreneurial support, financial inclusion, innovation transfer, and stakeholder coordination. title: Ranking, Not Point Estimates: Risk Tiering and the Case for AI-Assisted Loss Data in Caribbean SIDS Credit
summary: PURPOSE: To examine what physical risk information remains identifiable for credit in Caribbean Small Island Developing States (SIDS), where hazard data are rich but loss records scarce. DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: Using storm tracks and four damage-function calibrations, we assess Caribbean risk rankings through Monte Carlo simulation, stochastic dominance and independent records, and compare Caribbean and United States wind-loss relationships using wild cluster bootstrap inference. FINDINGS: Territory tiering is identifiable and broadly stable across damage-function choice, whereas point magnitudes remain imprecise under sparse Caribbean loss records. ORIGINALITY/VALUE: We identify an ordinal-cardinal boundary in Caribbean SIDS: risk tiering supports screening today, while precise loss estimates for pricing require better records that artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted methods may help develop. RESEARCH LIMITATIONS/IMPLICATIONS: Territory tiering can support risk screening, while data limitations motivate further research on AI-assisted loss-data generation for finer pricing. title: Sustainable Ecosystem Management for Biodiversity Conservation, Climate Resilience and Human Well-Being
summary: Sustainable ecosystem management is increasingly important for addressing biodiversity loss, land degradation, climate change, water insecurity and declining ecosystem services. Ecosystems provide food, freshwater, soil fertility, carbon storage, flood regulation, biodiversity habitat and cultural benefits that underpin human well-being. This article reviews the principles and approaches of sustainable ecosystem management and examines evidence from Rwanda to demonstrate the importance of integrated forest, wetland, soil, water and biodiversity management. Official national evidence indicates that forests cover approximately 30.4% of Rwanda, equivalent to about 724,695 ha, while wetlands cover approximately 276,477 ha. Rwanda has also reported an increase in forest cover from about 20% to 30.4%. However, the composition and condition of ecosystems remain important: plantations account for about 53.5% of forest cover, while natural mountain rainforests account for 18.1%. Wetland use is also intensive, with 74% reported as conditionally exploited, 6% unconditionally exploited and 20% fully protected. The evidence suggests that increasing ecosystem area alone is insufficient; management must also improve ecological quality, connectivity, resilience and sustainable use. The article proposes an integrated framework combining ecosystem assessment, risk analysis, restoration, sustainable land and water management, community participation, geospatial technologies, environmental governance and adaptive monitoring. Strengthening these components can contribute to biodiversity conservation, climate resilience, sustainable livelihoods and long-term environmental sustainability.

title: Can Nature Be a Legal Person: Perspectives on Rights of Rivers, Forests, and Ecosystems
summary: The growing ecological crisis, characterized by climate change, biodiversity loss, deforestation, pollution, and degradation of freshwater ecosystems, has prompted renewed debate regarding the adequacy of conventional environmental law. Traditional legal systems generally treat nature as property or a resource subject to human ownership and exploitation, providing protection primarily through regulatory mechanisms designed to control environmental harm. In recent decades, however, several jurisdictions have adopted an innovative legal approach by recognizing rivers, forests, ecosystems, and other natural entities as legal persons possessing enforceable rights. This emerging doctrine, commonly known as the Rights of Nature, represents a significant shift from anthropocentric environmental governance toward an ecocentric legal framework that acknowledges the intrinsic value of the natural world. This paper critically examines the evolution of legal personhood for nature from the perspectives of environmental law, constitutional law, jurisprudence, and comparative legal studies. It analyses the philosophical foundations of the Rights of Nature movement, evaluates judicial and legislative developments in jurisdictions including Ecuador, New Zealand, Colombia, India, and the United States, and assesses the legal implications of granting personhood to rivers, forests, and ecosystems. The paper further explores the challenges associated with representation, enforcement, constitutional compatibility, indigenous rights, property ownership, and environmental governance. Finally, it proposes legislative and institutional reforms aimed at developing a coherent legal framework capable of recognizing the rights of nature while balancing ecological protection, sustainable development, and human interests.

title: AI-powered capabilities are associated with green new product development through exploratory and exploitative pathways
summary: Abstract Purpose – This study aims to investigate the mechanisms through which AI‑powered capabilities influence green NPD in manufacturing firms. Specifically, it examines the dual mediating roles of green exploratory and green exploitative, and tests whether the mediating effect of exploration is stronger than that of exploitation in the AI‑green NPD link. Design/methodology/approach – Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory, this study develops a dual mediation framework distinguishing green exploratory (sensing‑driven opportunity identification) from green exploitative (seizing/transforming‑driven process refinement). Hypotheses are tested using survey data from 333 Chinese manufacturing firms across five high‑priority sectors. Hierarchical regression and bootstrapped mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 resamples) are employed. Findings – The results show that both green exploratory and green exploitative significantly mediate the positive relationship between AI‑powered capabilities and green NPD. Critically, the indirect effect via green exploratory is significantly stronger than that via green exploitative, supporting asymmetric mediation. The full model explains 54% of the variance in green NPD. Originality/value – This study makes three key contributions. First, it unpacks the mediation black box between AI and green NPD by specifying two distinct process architectures. Second, it challenges the “balance assumption” of ambidexterity theory by demonstrating the primacy of exploratory mediation in AI‑enabled green innovation contexts, thereby extending dynamic capabilities theory. Third, it provides a rigorous methodological template for testing dual and asymmetric mediation, offering actionable guidance for managers, AI vendors, and policymakers.

title: Artificial Intelligence‐Enabled Life Cycle Sustainability Assessment as a Tool for Sustainability Coordination
summary: ABSTRACT Firms increasingly use sustainability information based on life cycle assessment, yet coordinated and accountable action requires more than richer assessment. This conceptual article develops a literature‐informed model of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled life cycle sustainability assessment (LCSA) as a tool for sustainability coordination in corporate social responsibility and environmental management, corroborating and refining a provisional architecture through a structured integrative analysis of 138 works spanning LCSA, AI and digital assessment, sustainability management, and coordination and accountability research. The model distinguishes assessment, decision support, and coordination, and specifies six recursive coordination movements: signal qualification, cross‐functional interpretation, priority formation, trade‐off and tension handling, responsibility allocation, and follow‐through. It proposes five governance conditions for accountable use, including visibility, contestability, and capacitated ownership, and distinguishes literature‐supported elements from theoretical propositions. AI‐enabled LCSA can support coordinated sustainability action when analytical outputs and the configuration choices behind them remain interpretable, contestable, and connected to organizationalresponsibility.

title: The Consensus Trap: How Expert Agreement Can Conceal Decision Non-Closure in Corporate Governance Dr. Birgit Maria Kemphues | International Boardroom Studies | DNC-RP
summary: The Consensus Trap: How Expert Agreement Can Conceal Decision Non-Closure in Corporate Governance Dr. Birgit Maria Kemphues | International Boardroom Studies | DNC-RP Ten experts may agree. A board may approve. A transaction may proceed. Yet a fundamental question remains: has the decision itself actually been resolved? This conceptual research paper challenges the assumption that expert agreement necessarily establishes decision readiness in corporate governance. It examines how professional consensus, institutional authority, executive influence and formal approval processes may create the appearance of closure while significant decision conditions remain unresolved. The paper forms part of the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP), originated by Dr. Birgit Maria Kemphues. Drawing on more than 35 years of international business experience across Europe, Asia and the Gulf region, and exposure to decision-making environments in over 400 organisations, her research investigates the distinction between a decision that has been formally approved and one that can withstand independent scrutiny. The analysis develops a conceptual explanation of how expert agreement can reinforce authority, discourage further questioning and conceal unresolved assumptions, dependencies and accountability gaps. It considers alternative explanations and proposes directions for empirical investigation. At its centre is a governance question with direct implications for boards, chief executives, owners and high-stakes transactions: When everyone agrees, who is still examining the decision? The paper contributes to the developing DNC-RP framework by examining the relationship between expert consensus, organisational power, independent scrutiny and substantive decision closure. title: Development strategy in strategic enterprise management amidst modern economic turbulence
summary: The article examines the theoretical, methodological, and practical foundations of strategic management within enterprises amid global economic turbulence, heightened market uncertainty, accelerated adoption of digital technologies, and the conditions of martial law in Ukraine. It argues for transforming classical management models by shifting from traditional long-term planning to dynamic, adaptive strategic structures. It is argued that, in the current environment, an organization’s capacity for flexible strategic management has become a key factor in maintaining its viability and competitiveness. The study critically analyzes and systematizes existing conceptual approaches to defining “strategic management” and “strategic planning” (including classical, managerial, long-term, competitive, and communicative perspectives). It shows that integrating advanced technological solutions—such as artificial intelligence, cloud technologies, and big data analytics—creates new business opportunities while also introducing significant risks, including cyber threats and an urgent need to transform corporate culture. The paper emphasizes aligning digital initiatives with the enterprise’s overarching strategic objectives. The study focuses on strategic management in domestic enterprises during a systemic crisis triggered by military conflict. A fundamental shift in managerial focus is evident: a move from large-scale development plans to tactical, anti-crisis measures aimed at survival. The study identifies the primary adaptive strategies Ukrainian businesses used, including relocating production facilities, diversifying supply chains, optimizing operating costs, aggressively expanding into international markets, and unprecedented strengthening of risk management and corporate social responsibility. Based on the research findings, the study draws a conceptual distinction between strategy development—a process that requires open, creative thinking and focuses on identifying development directions—and strategic planning, which entails the structured, analytical detailing of the steps needed to achieve specific goals. The study argues that successful strategy development cannot be achieved without deep alignment with the existing corporate culture and workforce traditions. The study concludes that modern strategic management should not be viewed as a standardized, template-based tool but rather as a continuous, iterative process of creating unique competitive advantages. This process requires careful consideration of technological, macroeconomic, and internal organizational factors to ensure sustainable development. Keywords: economic turbulence, development strategy, strategic management during wartime, strategic planning, digitalization, crisis management strategy, corporate culture.

title: Executives with environmental backgrounds and corporate greenwashing: evidence from Chinese listed firms
summary: Against the backdrop of China’s dual carbon goals, corporate greenwashing not only misleads investors but also impedes substantive progress in green development. However, there remains a need to better understand how executives with environmental backgrounds influence corporate greenwashing through internal governance processes. Using a sample of A-share firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges from 2009 to 2023, this study empirically examines the effect of executives with environmental backgrounds on corporate greenwashing. The results show that executives with environmental backgrounds significantly curb corporate greenwashing. Mechanism analyses indicate that these executives reduce greenwashing by promoting substantive green innovation, improving environmental information disclosure quality, and mitigating managerial myopia. Further analyses reveal that this effect is more pronounced in non-heavily polluting industries and in information environments where the tone of media coverage is relatively negative. This study sheds light on the channels through which executives with environmental backgrounds affect corporate greenwashing and examines how industry-level environmental pressure and the external information environment shape this governance effect, thereby extending the application of upper echelons theory to corporate greenwashing research.

title: Blockchain Beyond Borders: Rethinking Tanzania's Legal and Regulatory Framework for the Digital Age
summary: Blockchain technology highly impacts on global financial systems, digital governance, trade, and data management, hence challenging the adequacy of traditional legal and regulatory frameworks that are largely territorially bounded. In Tanzania, the emergence of blockchain-based applications, cryptocurrencies, smart contracts, and decentralised digital platforms presents both significant opportunities and complex regulatory challenges. While Tanzania has made progress in regulating aspects of the digital economy through legislation on electronic transactions, cybersecurity, data protection, and financial services, there remains no comprehensive legal framework specifically addressing blockchain technologies and their cross-border implications. This article examines the extent to which Tanzania’s existing legal and regulatory architecture can respond to the realities of a borderless digital ecosystem. It argues that Tanzania’s fragmented regulatory regime risks creating legal uncertainty, constraining innovation, and limiting the country’s participation in the global digital economy. It proposes a forward-looking framework that balances technological innovation with regulatory certainty, financial stability, cybersecurity, and public interest considerations. Ultimately, it contends that Tanzania must move beyond reactive regulation and adopt a coherent blockchain governance strategy capable of addressing the opportunities and risks of the digital age.

title: The impact of sustainability certification on office rent levels: evidence from Prague
summary: Purpose This study examines whether sustainability certification is associated with higher office rents in Prague. While existing literature documents rent premiums in developed markets, empirical evidence from Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) remains limited. Design/methodology/approach Using a cross-sectional dataset of 125 Class A office buildings collected in 2025, this study estimates a semi-log hedonic model of asking rents as a function of location, certification status (BREEAM, LEED, WELL) and energy performance (the Czech PENB). Sixteen additional building and location characteristics are tested and found not to improve the specification. The analysis is complemented by location-specific Welch two-sample t-tests. Findings The results indicate a statistically significant certification premium of 8.8%, net of location and energy performance, which persists across all analysed submarkets. Unconditional submarket comparisons show larger raw rent differentials of 13%–17%, indicating that a substantial share of the raw premium reflects energy performance and location. The controlled estimate is comparable to premiums reported in mature Western European office markets, suggesting sustainability certification functions as an internationally consistent pricing signal even in a less mature CEE market. Originality/value This article contributes rare empirical evidence from the CEE region, specifically the Prague office market, with direct implications for valuation practice, investment strategy and ESG-related decision-making in post-transition economies.

title: A Sequential Foresight–Delphi Protocol for Diagnosing Anticipatory Legitimacy: Futures Wheel, Causal Layered Analysis, and Delphi Applied to Artificial Intelligence‐Powered Digital Government in Vietnam
summary: ABSTRACT Futures and foresight research offers mature methods for generating consequences, interpreting their meaning, and converging expert judgment, but rarely integrates them into fully specified protocols that diagnose an emerging technology's legitimacy risks before they materialize. This study develops and applies a Sequential Foresight–Delphi Protocol linking Futures Wheel consequence mapping, Causal Layered Analysis (CLA), and Delphi appraisal through prespecified transition rules, ex ante consensus criteria, a stability‐based stopping rule, and retention of dissensus. The protocol diagnoses anticipatory legitimacy, the prospective justifiability of AI‐enabled public authority, across consequential visibility, institutional responsiveness, and narrative alignment. It was applied in Vietnam, a critical illustrative case of compressed digital transformation, with a Quadruple Helix panel (26 invited; 20 completing every round). The panel anticipated efficiency gains cascading into accountability gaps, profiling, exclusion, and faceless administration; CLA traced the risks to a technocratic worldview and participant‐supplied images condensed as the algorithmic mandarin. Across two original Delphi rounds (urgency, feasibility) and two supplementary rounds (legitimacy‐enhancing potential), the panel converged on impact assessment, public registers, human review, and sandboxes, whereas contestability‐by‐design and independent audit reached consensus on urgency and legitimacy‐enhancing potential (for audit, without meeting the stability criterion) yet did not converge on feasibility, retaining the portfolio's two lowest feasibility ratings. We advance this asymmetry as an open–closed proposition for comparative testing. All claims concern expert‐anticipated consequences and judgments; no causal, predictive, or statistically generalizable claims are made.

title: Exploring the Potential of Rural Marketing in Bangladesh: Opportunities for Sustainable and Inclusive Development
summary: Rural marketing has immense potential to become a sustainable and inclusive development in Bangladesh since more than half the population is rural. The aim of the paper is to explore the implicit aspects that impact the growth and sustainability of rural marketing opportunities. The quantitative research design was the methodology applied, which included a questionnaire that was structured and 460 rural respondents represented various occupational groups, education levels, and income brackets. Data were tested using descriptive statistics, correlation, and multiple regression analysis to determine the most significant predictors of marketing opportunities in rural locations. The results indicate that the most significant effect on market growth is made by infrastructure development and government support, technology adoption, distribution systems, and consumer awareness have moderately significant impact. Nonetheless, growth is still hampered by structural factors like poor transport, poor financial inclusion, and unreliable implementation of policies. The analysis highlights that to unlock the potential of untapped rural markets, coordinated efforts that incorporate infrastructure, technology, supply chains, consumer education, and good policies are critical to achieving the desired outcomes. The insights are useful to businesses interested in market penetration, and policymakers who want to develop frameworks to enable inclusive rural development.

title: Do financial analysts improve the quality of earnings forecasting? Evidence from Central Europe, 2014–2024
summary: Purpose This study examines whether consensus analyst forecasts for annual earnings per share (EPS) are more accurate than a standard random walk (RW) model for companies listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange, the Prague Stock Exchange, the Budapest Stock Exchange and the Bucharest Stock Exchange during 2014–2024. Design/methodology/approach Consensus analyst forecasts for annual EPS from EquityRT are compared against RW model predictions using mean arctangent absolute percentage error, mean absolute error and mean square error. Wilcoxon and permutation tests assess statistical significance. For the Warsaw Stock Exchange, which provides the largest sample, the analysis is further stratified by analyst coverage intensity, firm capitalization, industry classification, corporate governance structure, institutional ownership composition and dividend orientation. Robustness checks employ alternative error metrics across multiple dimensions. Findings Consensus analyst forecasts for annual EPS demonstrate no statistically significant differentiation from RW predictions for Poland (excluding 2020), the Czech Republic (excluding 2020 and 2022), Hungary (excluding 2020) and Romania (excluding 2019 and 2022). This finding holds with respect to ownership structures and dividend policies. In the Polish market, for which detailed multi-dimensional analysis is provided, the absence of analyst advantages persists across annual periods, analyst coverage levels, firm sizes and industry groupings. These results challenge prior evidence of analyst superiority over statistical models in developed markets by drawing on a distinct market setting. Originality/value This investigation provides the first rigorous statistical examination of analyst forecasting performance across the major Central European capital markets, offering broader empirical insights into the boundary conditions of analyst expertise. The findings challenge the universal applicability of analyst superiority documented in developed markets, demonstrating that consensus analyst judgment provides no measurable advantage over RW benchmarks for annual EPS forecasting when market conditions exhibit RW earnings behavior. These results carry immediate implications for global investment strategies and resource allocation decisions, suggesting that expenditures on equity research may be misallocated in markets where fundamental earnings unpredictability renders consensus analyst forecasts no more accurate than RW benchmarks for annual EPS.

title: Unsettled temporalities: Deep-time governance and the politics of construction grounds
summary: The soil movements of construction form terrains of colliding temporalities. In southern Finland, clayey soils rendered surplus through construction are increasingly framed through the circular economy. Dominated by the tempos of construction timelines, urban growth and regulatory cycles, clay is increasingly forced into ever-accelerating capitalist rhythms. Drawing on scholarship on deep time and soil–human relations, this article examines how conflicts over these soils are not merely logistical or regulatory; they also reveal a temporal mismatch between the tempos of industrialised construction and geological rhythms. My findings show how dominant time practices compress geological temporalities, reinforcing anthropocentric and extractive logics. Additionally, the indeterminacy of clay complicates efforts to incorporate it into emerging frameworks of deep-time governance. As a political and temporal orientation for environmental governance, I propose a nuanced deep-time literacy, one that can recognise temporal dissonance, attend to the agencies of earthly matter and reframe soil rendered surplus, not as residue to be managed but as sites of ongoing negotiations around deep-time resistance and relations. The article contributes to a growing effort to reframe soil–human relations not as a managerial frontier for sustainability but as a terrain of ethical entanglement, ontological frictions and potential policy reorientation.

title: Regional institutional quality and the signaling value of legality ratings
summary: Purpose Drawing on signaling theory, this study investigates whether government-backed legality certifications influence firms' likelihood of experiencing high-growth episodes and the moderating role of regional institutional quality. Design/methodology/approach The empirical analysis is based on a longitudinal dataset of 115,679 privately held Italian firms, combining data from Analisi Informatizzata delle Aziende–Bureau van Dijk, the Italian Competition Authority, and the European Quality of Government Index. The observation period covers 2014–2022. Probit regression models are employed to test the hypotheses, complemented by a series of robustness checks, including propensity score matching, lagged specifications, and alternative econometric specifications. Findings The results indicate that Legality Rating (LR) adoption is positively associated with the likelihood of experiencing high-growth episodes, particularly in regions characterized by weaker institutional quality. Research limitations/implications The main limitation of this study lies in its exclusive focus on Italy, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other contexts. Practical implications From a management perspective, the findings underscore the importance of investments to strengthen compliance systems, ethical practices, and anti-corruption mechanisms. When formally validated through state-recognized certifications (such as the Italian LR), these practices can become credible signals of corporate quality, with positive implications for business growth. Social implications Legality certifications act as credible signals of organizational quality and integrity, underscoring the strategic relevance of corporate legality and ethical behaviour in promoting firm growth and enhancing stakeholder trust, particularly in weaker institutional settings. Originality/value By extending signaling theory to government-backed legality certifications, this study highlights the role of institutionalized signals of legal compliance in fostering entrepreneurial growth. It also provides novel evidence on the interaction between corporate social responsibility and institutional environments, contributing to the literature on high-growth entrepreneurship, signaling mechanisms, and institutional contingencies.

title: BETWEEN INCENTIVE AND OBSTACLE: ENVIRONMENTAL LEGISLATION AND ITS IMPACTS ON ORGANIZATIONAL SUSTAINABILITY – A SYSTEMATIZED LITERATURE REVIEW
summary: This research evaluates, through a systematized literature review, the main aspects of Brazilian environmental legislation that simultaneously function as instruments for promoting sustainability and as barriers to organizational competitiveness. The central problem investigated consists of analyzing how Brazilian environmental legislation acts simultaneously as an instrument for promoting sustainability and as a barrier to organizational competitiveness, especially in the national corporate context. The study aimed to examine the dual effects of legislation on innovation, competitiveness, and organizational ethics, investigating how regulations can promote sustainable development or limit business activities. Methodologically, this was a bibliographic study, based on a systematized literature review in databases such as SciELO, CAPES, and Google Scholar, with texts selected according to criteria of relevance, recency, and theoretical consistency. The results indicate that legal instruments such as the National Environmental Policy (Law No. 6,938/1981), the National Solid Waste Policy (Law No. 12,305/2010), and CONAMA resolutions have contributed to strengthening environmental governance, disseminating reverse logistics, and encouraging the pursuit of environmental certifications. However, challenges related to bureaucracy, legal uncertainty, and high compliance costs persist, hindering the effective internalization of a sustainability culture. Thus, although legislation is essential for ecological preservation, it has an ambivalent nature that requires greater integration with inclusive public policies and ethical and innovative business strategies.

title: AI-Automated Financial Reporting, Accounting Quality, Internal Controls, and Equity Market Valuations: Documentary Evidence from GCC-Listed Companies
summary: GCC corporate reports disclose growing use of artificial intelligence (AI), but finance-specific adoption is often mixed with deterministic automation and wider enterprise initiatives. This study examines what eight GCC-listed issuers report about financial-reporting applications, accounting quality, internal controls, and equity-market valuation. A deductive comparative case design applies manual documentary content analysis to 43 distinct evidence IDs across 51 register rows from issuer reports. Predefined categories identify deployed finance-related AI, non-AI reporting automation, adjacent control uses, prospective applications, and market context. stc describes an AI-based IFRS advice assistant with reported productivity indicators; other issuers document regulatory reporting automation, governance, fraud monitoring or control-testing systems without consistently identifying financial-statement AI. An internal GPT pilot described at stc includes Internal Audit users but is not evidence that GPT conducted an audit. Market capitalisation disclosures do not identify AI-related valuation effects. Findings support more precise disclosure of tasks, deployment, human oversight, and measured outcomes; causal impacts cannot be inferred from these documents alone.

title: Do bank branches always exert a positive impact? A perspective from commercial banks issuing wealth management products
summary: As fintech advances rapidly, the traditional functions of bank branches are increasingly challenged. Based on a sample of 127 commercial banks covering 2015–2022, this study explores how bank branches affect banks’ wealth management capacities (WMC). We find that bank branches are negatively correlated with banks’ WMC, which suggests that bank branches erode banks’ competitive edge in the wealth management market. Mechanism analysis suggests that higher operating costs are a potential channel through which bank branches are negatively associated with banks’ WMC. The moderating effect suggests that the cost effect arising from bank branches is weaker among banks with higher digitalization levels. We also find that the negative effect of bank branches on banks’ WMC is more pronounced for state-owned banks and larger banks. This study provides implications for policymakers and bank investors.

title: Knowledge‐Based Process Assurance: A Stakeholder‐Driven Framework for Internal Control
summary: ABSTRACT UK corporate governance remains on a largely “comply or explain” basis, despite continuing control failures. This paper proposes a Self‐Assurance (SA) paradigm—a decentralised, stakeholder‐centred, knowledge‐management process that embeds control ownership and testing within business operations. Using a conceptual governance lens, a portable SA framework is posited based on role identification within processes and key routines. This is developed through designing process maps and controls that identify risk and align control design with stakeholder needs and their risk ‘appetite’. Drawing on field applications when implementing a Financial Self Assurance process (FSA), observations are made on implementation challenges (culture, capability, systems, reporting) and practical countermeasures (explicit ownership, authority delegation, process mapping, targeted training, and dashboards). This leads to the view that FSA may be characterised as a knowledge‐led business‐friendly route to stronger internal control. The paper's contribution lies in the development of a pragmatic, scalable methodology for organisations to generate defensible control assurance while improving process performance and KM.

title: The influence of CSR and CKMC on new software product development and innovation capability: the moderating role of environmental dynamism
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine the impact of new software product development (NPD) on innovation capability (IC), taking into account the mediating roles of corporate social responsibility (CSR) and customer knowledge management capability (CKMC). It also examines the moderating role of environmental dynamism (ED) in the relationships between NPD, CSR, CKMC and IC. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 548 employees working in information technology (IT) small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across different organisational contexts in Portugal. A self-administered online survey was distributed via email and WhatsApp, enabling broad participation among respondents. The research model and hypotheses were tested using structural equation modelling with SmartPLS 4. Findings The findings reveal statistically significant indirect associations between NPD and IC through CSR and CKMC. ED positively moderates the relationship between CKMC and IC. However, it negatively moderates the relationship between NPD and IC and has no significant moderating effect on the relationship between CSR and IC. Practical implications This study offers practical guidance for SME managers by highlighting the importance of developing CSR and CKMC processes, particularly those related to capturing, analysing and applying customer knowledge to tailor services. Managers should prioritise the establishment of customer feedback integration systems, such as CRM analytics and user feedback loops, and align CSR initiatives with product development processes, such as eco-design and ethical sourcing. The findings indicate that firms that systematically use customer knowledge in NPD processes are more likely to enhance their IC. Originality/value This study offers a novel perspective by integrating CSR and CKMC as dual mediators between NPD and IC, a relationship that has not been extensively explored in the context of Portuguese IT SMEs. In addition, it examines how ED moderates these relationships. This research contributes to the innovation literature by offering a comprehensive, multilayered model that reflects the dynamic nature of innovation in rapidly evolving environments.

title: A Study of CSR Practices and Environmental Sustainability Initiatives of Major Industries in Rajasthan
summary: Rajasthan has some of India’s biggest mining, oil and gas, cement, and textile industries, each having to adhere to the mandatory Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) guidelines stipulated in section 135 of the Companies Act of 2013. This study looks at the four leading companies in the industries mentioned above—Hindustan Zinc Limited (Mining), Cairn Oil & Gas/Vedanta Limited (Oil & Gas), Shree Cement Limited (Cement), and RSWM Limited of the LNJ Bhilwara Group (Textile)—in terms of CSR expenditure and environmental sustainability practices. Using the sustainability reports and CSR reports of these companies in addition to literature on the topic, it is observed that the amount spent on CSR varies greatly among the different industries and even within an industry: Hindustan Zinc Ltd reports an expenditure of ₹273.45 crore in FY2024-25 while Shree Cement Ltd spends ₹51.34 crore on CSR in FY2023-24, while Cairn Oil & Gas’s multistate CSR expenditure decreased from ₹25.53 crore in FY2021-22 to ₹10.26 crore in FY2024-25. Similar variations have been seen in environmental initiatives: Sewage treatment and land restoration by Hindustan Zinc, Water positivity and renewable energy by Shree Cement and water conservation by RSWM through its Zero Liquid Discharge project.

title: Relevance of Technological Development To Economic Growth in Africa: A Position Paper
summary: Technological development is increasingly pivotal to Africa's aspirations for productivity, growth, structural transformation, and global competitiveness. This position paper argues that technology should be viewed as an essential component of Africa's economic-growth strategy. Technology can enhance productivity, slash transaction costs, expand market accessibility, back up financial inclusion and create novel economic opportunities. However, its merits depend on complementary investments in human capital, digital infrastructure, energy, research and development, finance and effective institutions. Recent evidence shows that digital infrastructure promotes innovation in Africa, particularly when supported by human capital (Osei, 2024), while technological innovation and human capital jointly contribute to industrial productivity and competitiveness (Awode & Oduola, 2024). The paper examines the major technological opportunities and impediments shaping Africa's development, including digitalisation, artificial intelligence, automation, fintech, smart agriculture, digital health and emerging mobility. It further highlights continuous challenges such as insufficient infrastructure, unreliable energy, limited digital skills, weak research capacity, financing constraints and institutional gaps. The paper argues that addressing these constraints needs coordinated policies that join technological development with education, industrialisation, entrepreneurship and inclusive economic transformation. Africa must therefore move beyond technology consumption towards technology adaptation, production and innovation. Empowering local technological capabilities and regional cooperation is necessary for ensuring that technological progress result in sustainable, inclusive and broad-based economic growth across the continent.

title: Adoption of AI-Powered Chatbots in Digital Financial Services: A Relational–Technological Model of Usage Intention
summary: The recent expansion of conversational artificial intelligence has driven the integration of intelligent chatbots into various digital spaces, progressively transforming how people interact with technology-based services and platforms, particularly within digital financial services and FinTech ecosystems. Although much of the research on technology adoption continues to focus on functional variables associated with system utility and performance, understanding the role of relational dimensions in human–AI interaction remains limited. In this context, this study analyzes the relationships between relational experience, perceived technological quality, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention to use chatbots, proposing a relational–technological model to understand the adoption of conversational systems in digital contexts. The research followed a quantitative approach with a predictive-explanatory cross-sectional design. The sample consisted of 398 users from Metropolitan Lima who had recently used AI-powered chatbots in digital financial services. Statistical analysis was performed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that relational experience showed significant positive relationships with perceived technological quality, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention to use AI-powered chatbots within the proposed structural model. Furthermore, perceived usefulness was found to partially mediate the relationship between relational experience and behavioral intention, although this indirect effect should be interpreted as complementary effect because of its modest magnitude. These findings suggest that the adoption of intelligent conversational systems is associated not only with the functional aspects of the system but also with users’ experiences when interacting with these technologies, highlighting the relevance of relational experience as a complementary dimension for understanding AI chatbot adoption in digital financial environments.

title: State policy strategy for the development of socially responsible partnership under war and post-war recovery
summary: This article outlines the strategic foundations for formulating and implementing state policy on developing socially responsible partnerships in Ukraine amid a full-scale war, structural transformations in the national economy, and prospects for postwar recovery. The relevance of this study stems from the need to identify new institutional mechanisms to reconcile the interests of the state, business, workers, local governments, civil society, and international partners, thereby overcoming the socioeconomic consequences of the war, preserving human capital, restoring employment, and ensuring the sustainability of local communities. Particular attention is paid to the limitations of traditional social dialogue mechanisms, which primarily focus on regulating social and labor relations and do not fully address contemporary challenges in economic recovery, responsible investment, social integration, and public accountability. The conceptual framework for a state policy on developing socially responsible partnerships is grounded in a people-centered approach, inclusivity and non-discrimination, subsidiarity, transparency and accountability, conflict sensitivity, mutual responsibility of the parties, and effectiveness. The framework is based on a people-centered approach, inclusivity and non-discrimination, subsidiarity, transparency and accountability, conflict sensitivity, mutual responsibility of the parties, and effectiveness. For each direction, the paper identifies priority tasks, instruments of state regulation, and expected socioeconomic outcomes. The paper proposes a multi-level mechanism for implementing state policy that coordinates management decisions at the national, sectoral, regional, local, and corporate levels. The paper explores opportunities for combining regulatory, economic, contractual, informational, and reputational tools to encourage responsible behavior among partnership participants. It focuses on integrating social responsibility criteria into mechanisms for government support, public investment, procurement, and recovery project implementation. The paper substantiates the feasibility of applying differentiated requirements to participants in partnership programs, depending on the scale of their activities, the nature of their projects, and the level of social and environmental risks. title: Smart City Pilot Policy and the Socioeconomic Dimensions of Sustainable Urban Development: Evidence from China
summary: Does China’s smart city pilot policy (SCPP) do more than raise economic output? This paper asks whether it also spreads development gains across regions and between urban and rural areas, treating the policy as a lens on selected socioeconomic dimensions of sustainable urban development. We study the 2012 SCPP on a panel of 167 prefecture-level cities from 2007 to 2022. A common prosperity index, constructed with entropy-weighted TOPSIS, measures overall prosperity, urban–rural integration, and regional coordination; the policy effect is estimated with PSM-DID. The SCPP raises the index by 0.0328 points in the fixed-effects model and 0.0304 points in the PSM-DID model with controls. The gains are uneven across dimensions: they concentrate in overall prosperity, appear weakly in urban–rural integration, and are not statistically detectable in regional coordination. Digital economy development and new-type urbanization both moderate the policy effect upward. Location matters as well: the effects concentrate in eastern cities and in cities with higher human capital and better informatization infrastructure. Local development conditions, in short, shape where the benefits of smart-city investment land.

title: ROLE OF HUMAN RESOURCES DIGITAL READINESS IN MODERATING DIGITAL MANAGEMENT AND CULTURE ON PERFORMANCE EFFECTIVENESS
summary: Digital transformation has become a strategic requirement for organizations; however, its failure rate remains high due to the gap between technology adoption and Human Resource (HR) readiness. This study aims to analyze the direct influence of digital-based management and organizational culture on performance effectiveness, as well as to examine the moderating role of HR digital readiness. A quantitative method was applied to companies and professional organizations in the fields of Human Resources and Human Capital (HC). The findings reveal that digital-based management does not affect performance effectiveness, which is largely attributed to low levels of digital literacy among employees. Conversely, organizational culture was found to have a positive effect on performance effectiveness. Moderation testing indicates that digital readiness is a prerequisite for successful digital transformation, however, HR digital readiness negatively moderates the influence of organizational culture on performance effectiveness. The implications emphasize the importance of organizational investment in enhancing HR digital readiness through targeted training programs to align competencies with digital systems. Theoretically, this study enriches the development of contingency theory in HR management. Limitations of this study include sample size and reliance on questionnaires which may present bias.
